title: Item binding — one archetype attached to one assessable unit
description: Governs content/competence/items/bindings/<domain>/<element-id>.yaml. A binding attaches an archetype to a specific (element x level) assessable unit and supplies what the archetype could not know: this element's parameter ranges, its tolerance, and why this shape tests this competence. Bindings are the cheap half of the item bank and there are roughly 9096 of them — hours of work each, not days. THE FAILURE MODE THIS SCHEMA EXISTS TO CATCH: a binding that is well-formed and an archetype that is excellent can still combine into an item that tests the archetype rather than the element. That defect is invisible in either artifact alone, which is why `justification` is required prose and why binding review is a separate quality gate rather than a rubber stamp on archetype review.

bindings.description: One entry per level of this element that has an item. The validator's coverage report treats an assessable unit with no binding as a gap: an element attainable at L4 with items only to L2 cannot actually be credentialed at L4, and that must be visible rather than discovered by a candidate.

level.description: Must not exceed the element's levelCeiling, and must be a level the archetype declares it can serve. Both are validator-enforced.

justification.description: REQUIRED. Why this archetype, bound this way, tests THIS element rather than the archetype's generic shape. This is the binding-review gate in one field. A justification that would read identically for a dozen other elements is itself the evidence that the binding is generic — reviewers are instructed to reject on exactly that signal. Name what the candidate has to know or decide that is specific to this element.

parameterRanges.description: Concrete draw ranges for the archetype's declared parameters, chosen for this element and level. Difficulty lives here: the same archetype serves L2 and L4 by what it is allowed to draw, not by being a different item.

datasetRef.description: Content-addressed reference to an archived dataset. Hashed so an item can be reconstructed exactly years later when a credential is re-reviewed.

toleranceOverride.description: Replaces the archetype's tolerance band where this element demands something different. A tighter band at L4 than L2 on the same archetype is normal and expected.

witnessRequirement.description:
What the witness must observe FOR THIS TEST that the finished record cannot show.

REQUIRED where the bound archetype is a `witnessed-performance`, and refused anywhere else — a submitted item has no witness, so a requirement on one is a sentence nobody will ever act on. The obligation is derived from what the binding targets rather than declared by its author, exactly as `positionNeutrality` is.

WHY IT LIVES HERE AS WELL AS ON THE ARCHETYPE. A witnessed archetype spans a family of procedures — the measurement methods cg-18 groups together are one such family — and what a witness has to watch is a property of the PROCEDURE, which the binding chooses. The archetype states what every test in its family requires; this states what this one adds. Keeping only the archetype's half would force every witnessed archetype to be written for a single test, and on an axis with 2732 equipment elements that is not a bank anybody can build.

The same test applies as on the archetype: name something the record cannot recover. "The candidate follows the procedure" is not an observation, it is a restatement of the task.

positionNeutrality.description:
REQUIRED by the validator when this element's knowledgeRefs reach a BOK section whose `consensus` is not `established` or `broadly-accepted` — that is, when the competence rests on something practitioners genuinely dispute.

State what the scoring credits and what it must NOT. On contested content a rubric may credit recognizing that the disagreement exists, declaring which reading the candidate is working under, using the evidence consistently with that reading, and conceding what the choice costs. It may never credit ARRIVING AT A PARTICULAR POSITION. A candidate who takes the other side and defends it from the records has demonstrated the competence, and a rubric that marks them down is scoring agreement with its author — which is a validity defect, not a strictness setting, and it is invisible in a rubric that otherwise reads well.

Discharge the obligation honestly where it does not bite: a binding at a level that never engages the disputed question should say so in one line. Silence and 'not applicable' are different claims, which is why the field is required rather than optional whenever the element reaches contested knowledge.

CI can prove this field exists and that the author considered the question. It cannot prove a rubric is actually neutral — that is binding review's job, and this field is what a reviewer reads first.

rubricRef.description: Rubric for this binding, where the archetype's generic rubric is not specific enough. Ships in the same commit as the binding.

review.description:
Who decided this binding was professionally valid, and what they concluded.

CI CAN ONLY PROVE A BINDING IS STRUCTURALLY POSSIBLE. It checks that the kinds match, that the level is within the archetype's declared range, that the parameters exist and that a generator parameter does not render. None of that reaches the question that decides whether the item is any good: does this archetype, with these parameter ranges, at this level, assess THIS element — or does it assess the archetype's generic shape while looking perfectly well formed? That failure is invisible in the archetype, which may be excellent, and invisible in the binding, which may be well formed.

REQUIRED BEFORE A BINDING MAY LEAVE `draft`, and not before. The parallel is rule 7: nothing above L2 rests on a draft element, because that is where independent work is entrusted. A draft binding is somebody's proposal and needs no signoff; a stable one is being served to candidates.

`reviewer` may not be an author of the element the binding targets, for the reason no-self-signoff exists: the person who built the thing is the last one who can tell whether it assesses something other than itself.

disposition.description: `disputed` and `rejected` are legitimate outcomes and both require a `note`. A binding a reviewer rejected is worth keeping in the record with its reason — the next author to reach for that archetype at that level needs to know somebody already tried.

note.description: Required when the disposition is `disputed` or `rejected`. What the reviewer thought the item would actually assess, which is the part a later author needs.

exposureGroup.description:
Bindings sharing a group are treated as the same exposure for control purposes, so a candidate cannot be served three near-identical items drawn from one archetype across adjacent elements.

IT NAMESPACES, IT DOES NOT COLLAPSE. Exposure identity is the group together with the exposure-relevant parameter values, so two bindings in one group still count as two exposures where their structural draws differ, and as one where they agree. It used to be the only lever there was, which meant a binding collapsed either all of its draws into a single exposure or none of them — decided by whether an author happened to write a string, with no rule anywhere about when to.
